Saturday's Tinto says:—The question, which it in evident there was no excuse for raising, will I. practically set at rest by the careful and patient letter from Sir F. I Roberts, which was yesterday read in Parliament. To cont. plain or a lien eel exposed to such dangers as were exhibited in the struggle of last Christmas for such measures of pre- caution as the proclamation of martial law for ten miles round Cabul is ridiculous. But British soldiers have always hitherto respected their enemies, and with the exceptions which the terrible passions of war occasionally provoke, hare been conspicuous for merciful and generous conduct. It should never have been hclieval that they conld hare acted at any different manner in Afghanistan, and the accusation has new boon conchreirelv refuted. The leaders of the . Opposition, it is undermloori, took counsel together yesterday upon the course they should pursue in respect to Afghan affairs. It in to he hoped they will resolve to show nn Countenance for the future to such imputations upon their countrymen as have in this case been finally disposal of. SPAIN. .

On Sunday, a train earning from Andalusia, conveying treasure to the amount of 40100 pesetas, which was placed ander the charge of a lieutenant and blur gendartnes, was Mopped by sixteen brigands between Alcasar and Argolis- idla. The bandits had blocked the railway by tearing up the rails and laying thorn across the line. Marshal Serrano happened to be a pamenger by the train, and brood the gendarme', with their commander, fired upon the brigands, who fled after returning the fire. After the excitement oconaioned by the attack had passed, it was found that one of the passengers had been injured by the madden stoppage of the trial, and that a gendarme bad been wounded by a shot. The gendarmerie are now in pursuit of the bandits. sWITZFRLAND. A celebrated murder trial hart just Leen brought too close in Geneva. On the night of March 1, 1879, the steamboat Simplon was lying at her moorings in a little bay near Belome, a village some five or six miles from Geneva, on the right bank of the lake, in charge of a man named Dumont stgi a boy, his eon. Shortly after midnight theV were roomed from their sleep by the harking of their dog, the boy went on deck, beet it Casino dark to see anything ; he fancied, however, he could hear, at some distant', from the shore, voices in dispute, which he conjectured might be those of quarrelling fishermen. Preening the incident of very slight importance, he returned to bed. Ten minutes later the dog began barking again, this thee more loudly than before. Ilte boy went en deck a second time, and looking over the side of the steamer he thought he could see small boat passing swiftly under her counter, and the same instant he beard diatinctly a voice on atm lake crying for help. . '' it snid ; "Icily, my liot.l, have pity." The elder Dumont now came on deck, and after shouting to the man in the water to keep up his courage, as they would be with him mete. minutes they went ashore, took the fleet boat they could find, and rowed swiftly in the direction in which they had heard the call for help. But they could neither me nor find anything, and after rowing about for A considerable time they returned to land, and reported to the moire and the police what had happened. The next morn- ing a man named Gine was miming from his home, ant seven days afterwards hia toile was found in the lake, and brought ashore bv. some fisher men. Foul play was suspected, and as public opinion accused Abraham Caron, a French deserter, who had halgril with liinet, of the crime, be and Oinet's wife were forthwith arrested and lodged in priwn in Geneva. After an itnprisonment of three months, Madame Gin. was released, while Caron, who had been kept in contineneut ever since, was lam week nut Ore his trial for the murder of Claude lintel. It was proved by the evidence of several witnesws that Caron bad horn on terms of sus- picious, if not of criminal, intimacy with Ginet's wife, and that he had written her a letter in which he had offered to relieve her of her husband. It appeared further that Caron had ebtained a great ai,cendancy over linnet, a man of weak character Alla intemperate habits, that he was always tempt- ing bier to indulge in his favourite vice and that on the day of (liners dismpeerance tlie Frmch deserter was the last person wen in his company. The theory of the prosecution we. that Caron, after plying his victiin with wine, had petanaded him to go with him on Ike lake in a boat which he found mimed to the quay ; that &sawn as they were out el earshot lie had fried to knock Gillet into the ;eater with en oar; that the latter resistril, and that it was only after • struggle, timing which one of the oars fell overboard, that he succeedel in his object. Caron was found guilty, but with extenuating circumstances, a qualification that has the effect of reducing by two years the fifteen years' impri- sonment, which is the uttnost punishment awarded by the law of Genet's. to the crime of wilful murder." ANOTHER ATTEMPT TO KILL THE CZAR.

I We have intelligenm from St. Petersburg of another aiablical attempt to take the life of the Czar by the explosion of a mine laid beneath a room% which the Imperial family were expected to dine. Through an accidental delay, however, they bad not aseembled when the explcuion took place, and the conspiratore therefore missed their object, but by the di.harge eight men of the Palace Coned were killed and 45 wounded. The ,ollowing telegrams have been received:— ST. PETEIISI3II., Tuesday.—An explosion •ook place to- day in the Winter Palace, but no member of the imperial fancily has been injured. The .nine by which the explosion hoe been effected was kid below the guardroom, which is situated under the dining hall. Thirty-tint men of the Palace (hard have been injured, and five have since died. The explosion made a hole ten feet long and six feet wide in the floor of the dining-roorn. Through an acci- dental delay the imperial fancily had not vet assembled to dinner.

So. Pe.nnteoerrno, Wednesday.--The following official an- nounceinent of the explosion at the Winter PaLee yesterday is published this morning —"At: about seven e clock yester- day evening, the title met., an explosion occurred in the basement of the imperial Winter Palace under the principal guardroom, by which eight of flee soldier. of the Finland Regiment of the Guard, then en duty, were killed and 45 others Injured. The flooring of the guardroom and , several gas pipes were damaged. An official inquiry is , proceeding." PHirEIMMAIII, Wednesday Afternoon.—An inquiry has been continence,' an to the circutifitances of the , explosion. The mine was placed immediately melee the , Guard-room, end was filled with dynamite and gun cotton. ; Three workmen were occupied in the MOM where.the explo- sion occurred, one of whom has taken tp flight. The train by which the exploeion Mar effected can be distinctly traced to the inner court and into the cellar, where a quantity of fuel was storrol. The fatunate postponeffient of the Car's , dinner hour was owing to the fact of hie Majesty haviii;l, gone to receive the Prince of Hesse. The epace in front of I [ the pdace is crowded by persons desirous of paying their , homage to the Car. Thanksgiving services have been held , in all the churches in St. Petereburg, and the city is gaily decorated with dags in honour of hie Mat,„e7;e ! Ilitattx,Wrolne;day.—The new, of the latest attempt upon !the Csar's life hag caused the most Intense excitement in this city. 'T he intelligence reached this place at about midnight. The Berlin newspapers keep issuing special editions on fresh I news is telegraphed from St. Petersburg, and the public Mimed is no keen that every flesh edition is bought up , almost as rapidly as it issues from the press. Messages tele- graphed from St. Petersburg fully admit the bolduess and , significance of the attempt, but they preeerve au abeolute ' eilence with regard to the author or authors, and nothing' whatever is known here as to the origin of the deed. The I German Emperor, upon teeing erdvised of the event, at once telegraphed a message of condolence and congratulation to his nephew, asking him for the fullest infortuation. Pants, Wednesday Night.—The news from St. Peterlarrg produced nothieg ehort of a coinmotion thin morning in Pafie It le felt here that the presed Cast's life is to some extent a 'malty for peace. Were he dead or dethroned the Emperor of Germany would be no longer withheld by family ties from executing the scheme of the war party in 80 force it would appiy to Russia. It is also felt that the reactionary forces will derive strength from the destructive spirit of the Russian Nihilist, tel that attemp. will he made to prove the French Republic solidoire with those insensate fanatics who blew up the Imperial dining-room yesterday in the Winter Palace. Already the Clerical Item here is endea- vouring to render odious in the eyes of the world the Milli, orderly, peace-loving, and thoroughly popular Government under which we live. There is not only no party in France in community of views or spirit with Nihilism' hut no organised group. Socialism inn Nihilist sense hirs in this country entered into the domain of ancient history, and the working classes here chiefly aspire by legal machinery to break down railway monopoly, oetroi custom, and to rotablieh a progremive mystem of taxation. No sooner had M. Urevy eddy this morning received in- formation of the ilot against the Cmr than he telegraphed congratulations to his Majesty, rod sent General Piffle to inmribe his name at the Russfan Embassy. The despatches received there are of a summary character, and sparing of distinct details. It is known that dynamite wan the ex- plosive used. The opinions of the French press are just what might have Leen anticipated before the evening papers appeared. The Republican organs express unfeigned horror. The reactionary organs, which place King and Pope above the mother country, insinuate that it is the fault of the French revolution. The Nationa, which is Governmental, saver). Nihilists obstinately pursue their guilty echeme. They have sworn to kill the Emperor.and the merest Lament has prevented their plot against his life succeeding. The Presse says this attempt must sodden all lovers of liberty. The rettrictive law, which will follow will unhap- pily find an excuse In the odious Nihilist agitation. The Fr.owe mys no historical crime affords a parallel to that of yesterday. The Union rays the monsters engaged in the plot recoiled not from the idea of widespread slaughter. Such wretches should Le excluded Dorn the pale of humanity. Whence comes this plague of regicide which poisons Europe ? Are the King-slaying fanatic. precursors of that social transformation which the apostles of revolu- tion complacently announce, and which has become the rallying word of European conepiratore? In the natne of what power have these abominable crimes been attempted ? , To ascertain, we have only to examine the doctrines of the revolution. There we discover wherein is the power of the ioidul7eZere'cla'y";l'igihtt!'e ;L"elonferthlir::4 the new. of the freeh attempt on the Czar's life reached the Quirinal than the King at once telegraphed to St. Petereburg hie horror at • the crime rod congratulation, to the Cmr on his miraculous rorope. "In doing no," say, the Fontana," the King only , expreesed the sentiment, of us all." The other journal,' without distinction, equally °epees. the ntrongest Indigna- tion. The Rifovna, while execrating Nihilist crimes, aaks whether punishment will repress the discontent extending from the dregs of the population to the steps of the Throne ; ! or should not the Czar, for his own sake, satiely the peoplee! legitimate aspirations? A DESCHIPTION OF.THE WINTER PALACE. Some particulare of the Winter Palace itself may not be uninteresting. It le described es the largest pileer in the world, being one-third larger than that of the Emperor of Austria, and unsurpassed in point of splendour. It is the residence of the Czar and his Court during the winter, and elands on tire left bank of the Neva,on the eilsoio house which in the reign of Peter the Great belonged to his [flak Admiral, Count Apraxin, who bequeathed it t. the Emperor Peter 11. It was so completely destroyed by fire in 1937 that it was I necessary to rebuild It, and one of the not least retnarkaale facts connected with it is that its preeent form was the work of two short years. The Palace is four storeys high, or about 30 feet. The fronbwe is 455 feet in length, and the breadth 330 feet. The principal entrance, or “perran des aut. bassadeurs," is front the Neva, and leade by a magnificent flight of marble steps to the State apartments of the Palace. A ptteway in the centre of HI building, facing Alexander's Column, ovens into a Large art. 'The most magnificent apartments are the Throne room of Peter 1., where the Diplomatic Corps generally present their congratulations on New Year's Day the White Hall, the Hall of St. George, a parallelogratn of 140 feet by 60 feet, the Gallery of the Field Marshalls, and ton Alexander Gallery. EXECUTION AT MANCHESTER. William Cassidy was on Tuesday executed at the Strange- ways Prison for the murder of hie wife, its Manchester, on the nth November last. Hoportere were again excluded, and the Coroner, finding that they ',mild not be admitted even Lke formal inquest if it was held within the prison walls, determined to hold his inquiry at an adjacent hotel. The jury appended co their verdict, whia was in the usual form, the following presentment, which the Corn er undertook to forward to tine Home Secretary The jury beg to exprese a wish that at future executions reporters of the press should be allowed to be preient." The prisamer and the murdered woman had been married about thirteen veers, and during the last months of their married life differences had arisen between then, whkh re- lofted in the display of considerable violenee on the part of I the culprit. On Saturday, the Bth !seconds., ISIS, ca,„..dy had hie meals at home, and subsequently went to the Nelson Inn, where he m esided over a "free and easy." The deceased woman went to, bed that night about I and her husband I left the pubbc-house about the same tune, but whether he I went straight home or not has not been aecertained. About one o'clock on the Sunday morning, a policeman who was paring Cassidy's house in Susan-street, liochlalesroad, bad his attention called to the bedroom Wisdom-, through which he saw dames. The officer booked at the door, and after he had knocked some time it was opened hr the culprit's son, a little b,y eleven years of age. On gaining admittance to the house, the constable I went upstairs. On the top he met the deceased, who was I quite nude and whoee body wan badly burnt. The constable went into the bedroom, where he found the bed in flames.l He promised water and extinguished the Ire, and when he went downstairs he saw the deceased partially dressed. the' was taken to the Infirmary. where she died early on the following morning. The deceased made a statement at the I Infirmary, in which she said she went to bed about half-pant , ten. i'Vhen she awoke the found herself in flames. She , , heard her husband going downstairs, sal cal I ,d to him, but ; , got no answer. She went downstairs where she found her I husband sitting boa chair, and awake. The falicomn was I there, and some aeighbours afterwards came it An ex- amination of the bed won afterwards made, and it was found that it must have been tiet on lire in several places. and the bedclothes were saturated with paraffin. Al :he trial, Mr. Nash, who defended the culprit, urged the jury to discharge him, on the ground that the prosecution had not made out a case and his l.nrdship, in summing Of,, pointed out that . several parte of the deceased's statements must be inaccurate. , judged from the evidence of several of the witness,. Cas- sidy declared that he was as innocent of the crime as ' Hiisren waa of the murder of Police-constable Cock. In Innen-ix—Thursday's Times my,: —The more the subject is regarded in all its as- pects the more plainly does it appear that direct aid to keep the people from starving and te enable them to prepare their land for another season is the least objection- able method of dealing with a difficulty that connot be ignored. In this way, while Parliament is making no extra- ordinary haste with the Relief Bill, the Duchess of Darlhorouglis committee has done, and is doing, admirable work, and we are glad to believe that the impartiality and prudent care with which her Grace, and those who are work- ing under her, have performed a delicate and arduous task, are generaliy reco;nised in Ireland. In former years in the inconvenient and dingy premises in Market-street con- siderable difficulty was experienced in delivering the extra number of letters and packages usually at St. Valentine's Day placed in the custody of the post office. The number of valentines uosted at St. Helens exceeded that of last year, end the work was accomplialled with comparative eme, the men commencing duty at four o'clock in the morning, Iwo hours before the usual time., and finished about half ao hour behind their usual time. ANOTHER ATTEMPTED LSSASINATION OF THE CZAR. Navas, surely, has a head that wore a crown mese cause to rest uneasily than has the Emperor of all the Ruseias. Another terribly cold-blooded and cruel attempt has been made int his life—an attempt equally cruel and murderous as the one that narrowly missed its mark at MOSCOW lom than three inonths ago. No doubt on this occasion, as on the lass, when a mine was fired in front of the Royal train, the destined victim wan the Czar ; hut in order to accomplish their object the amassine do not hmitate about the sacrifice of other lives. In the Moscow train there were several membern of the Imperial family, and on Tuesday the intention was to blow up a family dinner party, which, it is said, must have included the Duchess of Edin- burgh. It seems slmoet incredible that each an attempt should have been made, so similar in many of its details to the last, notwithstanding all the extra precautiam that have sinee been taken to, as it were, hedge round the person of the Emperor. It appease that a mine charged with dynamite and gun cott, was worked below the guardroom of the Winter Palace at St. Petersburg, and which is right under the Imperial dining-room. At the time of the ex- ploaion the Czar aud hi n family, bet for an accidental circumstance, would have been at dinner. Fortunately they had not assembled at the imtarit that the mine was fired, and no escaped uninjured. But ten

of the soldiers, who were in the guard- room undonieath were killed and forty•five wounded, and the forece of the expl. aim was no great that a hole was made in the .Uning-room ten feet long and air feet wide. An examination of the premises after the explosion revealed the fact that a train had been laid from a cellar where a quantity of fuel had been etered, to " the inner ccorrt ; " but how such elaborate preparations could have been carried oat in secrecy unknown to the police authoritien in indeed a my. tcry. The feeling of horror that this most extraor- dinary,outr•ge will give rise to all over Europe will be intense, and it will be equalled by one of out:abb. meat at the immunity with which the conspirstors were:enabled to work, notwithetanding all precaution.. It is stated that the utmost care has been alwayn oh. Boned in watching the imperial rooms. The Emperor's body-guard is ow duty day and nigot, end " anybody entering the bedroom or the library would hare to pass 200 Connacht." The moet:curiour thing in connection with this Nihilist conepiraey is that no reliable informatio• CAll be obtained as to its extent. It may be • very clamorous orgenteation an some believe, or it may be the work only of • desperat.aand dmpairing feve ; tot in either case the inability of the Russian authorities to deal with it by metieuree of represnion is bc,w-eog every day more manifest. Lt is known that the vast umjority of the Ruaalto people—of the peasantry--are still almoet superetitiouely affectionate in their loyalty to their Czar, and this irreconeileable hatred of the Im- perial Gevernment loss its origin in a species of "young Russian " party, semi•ednaated, imbibing new idea., and that the program of events, in 8.140. during the lam qnorter of a century her exeited to tho, kighesO pith a revolutionary Raney. The result of the Muluow plot veim the moforeang of a system of ro. preesion and rieletoe that cut off all niepee of libeml reform, and it it to I. feared that this fait attempt, will stimulate the Russian caurt to omumel a policy of no surreorlet to oonstitutional demands, arel of dogged etreugthening of obi...late power. The hounds of freedom aan pity the Raulne people who, butween Devotion and Nihilism, cannot easosed in valuing liberty, hut intense aympathy roma also be felt for the supeeiree chief of the state, the liberator of thy Serfs, attacked by a party whose policy in assassinatioth sad towarda whom ha mama dimplay leniency suspicions of weaklier., that would load to the destruction of 030 Imperial Goveaternent and the breaking up ei the Rneeian Empire.

div.head: TOWN TALK.
div.p: TOWN TALK.

The Chairman of the Widnes Local Board referred too somewhat singular fact at the last meeting of that body, viz., Chef though there had been such a terrible outcry about the quantity of rain which bad fallen during the year 1879, it appeared that, so far as Widnes at least was concerned, it bad only htfan 29.18 inches as aguinst 33-71 for 1878 ! I regret to hear that the company who are carrying on the Coffee ant Cocoa Room movement in Runcorn will not be able Co declares dividend at the annual meeting, which will be held on Monday. A dividend of 2i per cent. will be declared at the half- yearly meeting of the Runcorn. Weston, and Halton Water- works Company. It is gratifying to our that the affairs of this company are beginnidg to improve. At the ineeting of the Widnes Board a communication was read from the Local Government B...ird expressing their ! sense nf the activity shown by that body in doing all in , their power to prevent the spreading of zymotic diseases. In the course of some remarks on the improved health of the district, Mr. Carey paid a well-deserved compliment to the energy and care shown by Mr. ffickaon, the nuisance in- spector, in preventing the apread of such dixesses iu the dis- trict.

A somewhat retnarkable quietude is at present observable in police matters in Widnes. During the week there have ! been very few cases for trial, and these of a very unitnportan character. For long 'riffle iIISOCCtOr Bereft and his men have bad t terrible strain put upon them, not it is to be hoped after the execution of the priwners just sentenced to death, that a respite, at least, will be granted to the town from cases of lawlessness. No doubt the working popula- tion is of a very rough description, and hard to manage but a few more salutary examples, if need be, will have a wonderful effect in making the roughs a little more prudent.

It is very satisfactory to find that the various departments of the works under the superintendence of the Widnes Board are to he placed in telephonic communication with each Other, by the Edison Telephone Company, in consideration of certain privileges granted to them for passing through the • district. :Cot a very had bargain on the part of our local Ikgislators. The lecture delivered a few evenings ago by Mr. W. S. Caine, under the auspices of the Widnes Liberal Association, preyed a success. There was a capital attendance, and the information given by the colorer on our nientifie frontier in Afghanistan will prove invaluable to all opposers of the " gunpowder and glory " policy. Mr. Cahn is • very graphic and interesting speaker, and his exposure of the Caselessnese of many of the suggestions of the Russo- ' phobists was received with delight and applause by his hearers. The quiet satire with which he demolished the various bugbears of these alarmists was intensely interest- ing. div.head: REPRESEIg CATION. OF MID-CHESHIRE.
div.p: REPRESEIg CATION. OF MID-CHESHIRE.

... , . Sir,-1 ern not a voter in Mid-Cheshire, but in South-East Lancashire, my qualification being eituate not far from the I anks of the Mersey ; hence, being a near aeigllbOne, I have watched with some interest the growth and the rapidly- improving prospects of Liberalism in your division of the county of Cheater. I understand that Cl the opprambing general election yea have one excellent man ready to take the field in company of a imitable col leave; and the object of this letter is to suggest that the Lib,ale of need not go for a-field to find that suitable colleague. You have in your own division a gentleman wlmbad the courage to champion the Ltberal CAW. when its chances of success were—as compared with what they now are—exceedingly remote; a gentled.en who may be said robe the leading spirit amongst • band of earnest ani active Liberals, who are now, and have been for aome time past, workiag with a determine- tioa to make the return of two Liberal representatives not only possible, hut pro Sable, if note cerMinty. I need hardly say I refer to G. W. Latham, Est., of Bradwall Hall, Sandbach, to whose condidature, whenever Mid-Climhire was again contested, I have looked forward ae a matter of course ; hence, I was quite prepared for the enquiry of your correspondent, A Mid-Cheshire Farmer," who says, " May I ask how it ie Mr. fathom is not put forward ?" anddhen goes on tn.'s,. He (Mr. Latham) 15 the right her. to run," that "after six years of Tory Government the farmers have learned a 4.00 of what they (the Tone.) have done for them," end assures Mr. Latham that now," he is thought the champion of the farmers' cause." Sir, people now say that at loot the farmer iegathering up courage and beginning to have confidence in the remove of the ballot, but hem lee farmer who writes as if his next vote will be cast in record- coot with his convictions irrespective of the ballot, and, as we know that men's convictions have been ripening fast during the not three ye-ars. I should like to ask your readers the two following queations:—Will not Mr. Latham's able, honest, and fearlese advocacy of Liberal principles be more acceptable to your 'amines" men in towns than the inerthe of tbe two county ornamema who now one-represent them by giving a blind, a silent, aye and a servile, support to the Government of Lord Beaconsfield ? div.head: STRIKES v. ,ARBITRATION.
div.p: STRIKES v. ,ARBITRATION.

Sir,—l have lean favoured in receiving Sc this morning's post a copy of your issue of Saturday last, and when perusing its pages I found that it contained a letter written by some person who, for some reason best known to himself, has chosen to adopt the singular title of " Balltengs." For many years! wasconmelled, by force of circumstances, to use bentenge, and having always used them to the best of my humble ability, believe me 1 was somewhat surprised to find that I had laid myself open to the anitnadversions of an old acquaintance. The writer of the letter referred to has mustered up just sofiMent courage to inform your readers that he differs Iroin certain opinions expressed by moot the meeting of ironworkers, recently bold in Warrington. Difference, of opinion, when suppented by honest convic- tions, is without questi. n fairly debateable matter ; hut for myself, being plain and open in all my dealings with both mes and masters, I have a great aversion to occupy space in the pages of a newspaper to debate with a person who deems it necessary to seek shelter behind a nom de plume, who has not the courage or the honesty to eonie from behind the hilltongs in defence of the position which he assumes to be better than mlne. When at Warrington I may have said something which, if sulanitted to the crucial test of reason, might be found to he erroneous. The most educatwl thought that man can boaPt ot is liable to error, but what I did state on that occasion was stated by me with the best intentions. If the late advance in wages in Staffordshire was dispropor- tionate to the advance in the price of iron, the blame, I repeat, If anyone is to he blamed, rests more with the employers than with the arbitrator; and, in addition, you will please permit mete state that, although the advance was not so large as we had a right to expect, my faith in the wisdom and the justice col arbitration as a means of adjusting diffe- rences with respect to work and wages remains unshaken and if the principle of arbitration is good for the trade in a single county, it moat be good for the trade in the whole of the counties. Rot if .13alltongs " bee more faith in the wisdom and the justice of strikes and lockouts, and seriously believes that they are a more prolitable may Of adjusting differences in the iron trade than naving recourse to arbitration, perhaps he will ! I gnod enough to inform your readers what good was gained, and AISO what were the special benefits that the I ironworkers derived from the L. 50,000 which they spent on strikes and lockouts doing the eight years ending with 1870? And if the principle of regulating wages by the selling price of iron is not the hest, malty besides myself will he pleawd to be informed Sc "Dalltongs" what principle would be better.—Please insert this reply in your next issue, and oblige, yours most respectfully, JAMES CAPPER, . _

div.head: BESMICK REMOVAL CASE.
div.p: THE BESMICK REMOVAL CASE.

..... should not have troubled you with any contribu- tion to the Remick removal case controversy had it not been for the somewhat mysterious reference to "the misdon of alr. Handley "in the letter of Mr. J. C. Sutton appear- ing in your last issue, and which untler the fogginess of its phraseology seems to imply either ignorance or untruth on my part. he remark made by me at the last meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardims, "Theo the Wanington Guardians will have a good sum to pay," wan, I tneekly venture to my, warranterl by the facts which called it forth. Mr. Sutton says, "As a matter of finance the advantage is with my Union, the mission of Mr. Handley notwithstand- ing," but adds nothing in proof of his assertion. According to his own letter Beswick's children were chargeable to the Warrington Union on October 22m1, and as they were not removral to Dutton Workhouse until December 18th, this embraces a period of eight weeks. As Once weeks' mainte- nance only was claimed fro, and paid by the Runcorn Union, it would appear to any ordinary individual that the Warrington Union must have paid the remaining five weeks maintenance (unless Mr. Sutton has evolved out of his ac- knowledged superiority neon Union Clerk some new and secret WAy of doing so). I think I may mid, without betray-u ing the secrete of a clerk's office, that considerable expense is incurred and paid by Guardians for the preparation of the needful evidence in settlement and removal cases, rind the obtaining of magistrates orders for removal, md that not infrequently no special fee is awarded the Clerk for these extra services, a proportion of these expeig,s added to the cab hire, and the unrecovered five weeks maintenance, I sub- mit justify the remark made by me. The only advantage to the Warrington Union as a matter of finance is apparently the payment of an amount which might have been iv great part avoided had the inexpensiveaml common sense practice of many clerks to Boards of Giurdians been adopted by Mr. Sutton.—Yours respectfully, WILLIAM HANDLEY. Runcorn, Feb.ll3tb, 1880.

WINSFORD IMPROVEMENTS. Sir,—Not long ago Christ Church of this town was much delapidated, and was put under a course of improvetnents, but not a minute too sown. Bet it was hardly rmdy for re-opening before a fresh evidence of its insecurity and renewal dehipidations became manifest New, for a while remedial measures have been taken with the Market.place. Its houses, shops, and even Town Roll have either gone or are fast going. Many have been renewed, polled down, rebuilt, or arc left down, or fast are going down, so that they who have no property may be eaid to be blessed. Bob under private influence and Local Board sway, changes have boon going on for the better. The whole place is or has altered, property looks better, except the dwelling- houses, which it does not pay to rebuild. The street and its shom and publim shame the old market hall. Even parapets and drains are now along its sides. Some parte of the town boast of tiled .tuiseways, so tlmt one can past along —even on wet days—without getting over the shoe tops in dirt and numb. It feels quite like some civilised place,when one ca n I eavv the station Ind pass Meng f roni ravel tip to Over without hardly getting off tiles°, wetting one's booM. But how different if, on, wet clay, one wants to reach Swanlow-lane, and so paw up Weaver-street, still under the old manage- ment, it would seem—the little cut off must be at the expense of much dirt from the detestable cinders with which, as of yore, they will persist in botching up the causeway and street. They who live there have surely as much right as those in other parte to have tidy causeways and flrm, good streets. llow much better it would be to show the rate. payers of Weaver-street that their chore of the rate. did not go to improve every part of the town, and have their own part untouched, or worse than untouched, botched with cin- ders and clinkers, instead of a little mamdain and tiles for their causeway, like the rest. Than as to Dingle-lane and Way's-green, they are neglected altogether, or next door to it. Any improvement, that dangerous dough would soon tell its tale upon the vicinity and the accidents that might be (and the wonder is there have been no serious ones) would never occur. Surely tie better to avoid lose of life at a little doo expense than to lose it and then improve.— Tours, J. Winsford, February 18th, 1880.

Lannert. OF-anie an °TER.—We are sorry to record the death of the Hee. John Marshall, who for a period of above fifty years was pastor of the Congregational Church, Over. He retired from active duty about tour years ago, to ; the great regret of his large and influential congregation, but still continued teetered the chapel, reside in the booth, and take an interest generally in the manadement of affairs. After atinre his health began to fail, andafter some various fluctuations he was taken much worse, and expired on the morning of the IPtli net. When he began hit ministry there was no chapel,and services were held tea cottage. After a time he congregation increaaed, and what is now called the Old Chapel was built. In 186 T the present handthme stracture was erected, and was opened entirely free of debt. When Ile. Ofarshall had been pastor for fifty y.rs a jubilee service was held in one of the large rooms of Mr. Vaigh's factory, and an illuminated address and about £.600 were presented to him, ne a alight testimonial of the love and esteem in which be was held by his own people and every one connected with him. Ile was looked open as • father by the young, and as a friend as well as a pastor by the old ; both rich aud poor looked up to him as a spiritual and temporal adviser. Mr. Marshall was never married, but he leaves a large circle of friends to regret him.

NOTICII To Qrs-r.-11L—lirn; been settled law that in order to make a notice to quit valid it must be definite, and I not optional. If a landlord were to give • tenant notice that he would he at liberty to quit at • certain time mentioned in the notice, if he (the tenant) thought proper to do so, the teoant could not he compelled to give up posseesion, because the option was offered to him of going or staying. Thin is an extreme case, but it has occurred as also have numerous cases of all intermediee shades of difference, un- til at lest the limit lms been reached, fur the present, in a recent case. The circumstances were these. A land- lord gave notice to hie tenant to quit at a certain time, and, an far, the notice was admitted to be good. But the notice contained additional werds, offering teems fora new tenancy, and this addition to the notice cooed much trouble and expense. The tenant, being aware that an optional notice was invalid, refused to give up possession of the premises on the expiration of the notice. In the meantime the landlord had agreal to let the property to another tenant, which agreement he WWI tataVe to perform in consequence of the old tenant's retool to leave. The landlord thereupon com- menced an action of ejeetmeut against the old tenant, and the expectant tenant brought an action against the landlord for specific perfortnance of the agreement to let, and oleo for damages for breach of contract in not giving him poasession of the premises a the appointed titne. Both actions were tried, and to both the judge told the noti. to be bad, as being ambiguous and optional , and judgment was given against the landlord in bath actions. The landlord appealed, and after the case had been fully argued a majority of the Lords Justices hold that the notice was sufficieW. am: therefore reversed the previous decision in both actions. 'llia shows the importance of simplicity. If it be necessary to give notice to a tenant that is rent is to Le increased, tirst give him an absolute notice to gait; and after that is served, the first off, of ann. tenancy, at an increased rent, may be made to the tenant in possesaion. 'The neglect of this simple precaution, in the Instance now under consideratimj, nova. cloned two trials and two appeals and afterall the question cannot be considered to be settleti, as the judges were dividol is, opinion. What the result might have been if the question at issue had been taken to the House of Lords it is of course imposAble to say. Probably the decision of the Court of Appeal would have been upheld, and the sufficiency of the notice established but it is not wise to run the risk of becoming involved in costly litigation be following a form of nonce which has cabsod ciA •great difference of opinion among the judges... . . .

Mr. IL Neumann, the chairman of the North- with Local Board, presided, The room was c.owded to earners, and the proceedings were characterised throughout by the most uproarious condg&t. For several boors pre. ceding the meeting placate and handbills had been circulated, calling open ratepayers to be patent at the meeting to vote against an increaseof rotes. and the moult was that the middle and back portion of the audience wan entirely composed of dissentients to resolutions that were brougld forward. Mr. Neumann. on entering the room, ascompanied by Messra Weston and Hugheeand Mr. Cowley (sleek to the Local Board), were received with an outburst of cheers and groans.—The Chairman told the audience that he wee present in his official capacity as chairman of the Local Board, a requisition having been presented to them, calling upon them to convene the meeting, and therefore he would not express urn-opinion whatever upon the qutstion of adopting the Act for Northwich.—Mr. J. He proposed the adoption of the Act in that town, calling attention to the benefits and advantages that would inevitably accrue there- I front, and expatiating largely on the successful formation of free libraries in other towna—Mr. Ward said he honoured the • hody of persons preaent but they would honour hint more it they voted for the resolution. They were causing an up- I roar against a echeme which would only cost them half a farthing per week. surely they were not no poor, but they , could pay that. The advantages' derivable from such an institution were indubitable, and he hoped that none would vote against the motion, lie se- conded most cordially the resolutions-At this juncture gentleman iose up in the middle of the room to make some observations, when he AAS suddenly mopped by the cries of platform.' A portly gentleman NVAS next *beer :est making hie way to the platform in the midst of , uproar and applause. On his declaring himself to be in favour of the scheme, a storm of groans ensued, in which cries of "contract job" mingled frequently. He could not proceed for groans, but stolidly iteclared that he would s hare his may," which the aodience at last allowed hint, and he left the platform with a conscious smile of triumph. A prominent member of the Local Board, who was waited on the platform, followed with • speech. in which he enumerated , Ike advantages to be derived from the library. Much diversion and interruption was caueed by some ventriloquist, ! who by throwing his voice about the room, very persimently denied the accuracy of the gentleman', statementa. The speaker at last breathless and exhausted woo forced to sit down. Mr. Brunner and other gentlemen addr....l the, meeting, and the chairman ultimately put the resolutioo. when about a damn in the front held up their hands for the re-lotion, and an overwhelming majority against. - - DIMITE B 811•112 ST 'MONET LEITD6B4 AT Sr. HALESS. —At the Liverpool ASPiAkT, on Tuesday, the ease war tried in the Nisi Prim, Court. before Lord Justice Brett and a common piry. of Simmons,. Brindle and the hfanctiester Loan, trc., Company.—lt was en action hy Lewis Simmona money lender, Liverpool, to recover damages for breach of agreement by the defendants in wising the goods of Henry Morecroft, collier and provision dealer, Old Moss Houser Parr, St. flelens.—Mr. Q.C., and Mr. Bigham (in- etructed by Mr. Nonlon) were for the plaintiff ; Mr. Ruesell, Q.C., and Mr. Addison for the defendant Brindle ; and Mr. Pope, Q.C., and Mr. Taylor far the loan company.—The plaintiff and the defendants had lent money . Morecroft and had bills of sale upon his furniture. The instal- ments not being regularly ',aid, the loan company made a seizure, but they agreed to give up possession and not to seine again until the plaintiff's loan, amounting to £llO, had been paiil off. Notwithstanding this agreement, they shortly afterwards made another seizure and sold More- croft's furniture. The company sent a Mr. Wood and two men to take possession, and upon their arrival Morecroft comm.& Owl with Simmons, who seat four men. The result of the meeting of the rival bailiffs wee that Mr. Wood returned to Manchester with a black eye. The principal question in the case was whether Mr. Brindle, who was one of the direSors of the Manchester Loan Company, had authority to tnake the arrangement he dill with the plaintiff not to seise again until plaintifVe loan, amounting to LllO, hen been paid Lordebig, after hearing the evidence, ruled that such authority had been given, and directed the jury, with reference to damages. that a discount should be made for the plaintiff receiving the money now and at the time when his loan would probably have been repaid. The jury reterned a verdict for the plaintiff for £6O against the company —llia Lordship, in the action ageing Brindle, directed a verdict and gave judgment for the defendant.

EMIT on lAntskausx at. NreOttOP., Sn. Etatatne. —An emay ‘tas given on Liberalism M the Nutgrove Wes- leyan School, on Wednesday night, by Mn. Williain Foulkes, of. Matto Heath. Mr. Ellison occupies" the chair, and there was a goad attendance.—The emayist, after a few prefatory remarks, inquired the mmning of the word " Liberalism." The way in which it was formerly treated, and is treated at the present day by a great many people, would lead one to think who had never examined it himself that Mere is some- thing detectable in the principle—a something that was re- pulsive to our better nature, and which ought to be stamped out at any cost. Ile need hardly say that his opinion was in direct opposition to that; for he believed that its principles had embodied within then] some of the rnmt essential traits lore Christian character, and without which we could never attain to true manhood—the very thing he hoped they were all aspiring to. He believed that it its principles were pro- perly carrital to their legitimate end, the golden rule,. Do unto others as ye would inen should do to you," would be the out- come. Meu were apt to base their morality on the prevailing lawsof the land, and, from what we knew about some of them, they were anything but right., especially If the game law and the bankruptcy law were to be taken as specimens for our guidance. A good many of the laws A.emetl to be made for a favoured few, and not for the good of the majority, as they ought to he Speaking in reference to Liberalism, it was a matter of very great astonishment to him that its progress Baud been so ,low, especially with respect to its acceptance by the werking classes. Great benefita had been conferred upon them by the carrying out of Liberal principles during the last fmty .d fifty years. Various reetrktions upon com- mercial aml ,eanufacturing industries had been removal. Political restrictions had been imposed upon them by the Tories. and held on torn with an iron hand, notwithstanding their boasted assertions to the contrary. He almost felt appalled at the Idea that they should sit, so to speak, with their arms folded while their liberty was being stolen away from them, as they had been during this last period of Tom rule, and all throhgh faults of their own in not using theft privileges as they might do. Ile had tried to account for thia lethargy in the Liberal ranks. One of the came* Was that people dial not ',wow what Liberalism was, and, worse than that, lie was afraid they did not care. When some of them were talked to on the subject they appeared to be quite indifferent, widch was almost lamentable when thew coo, sidered the tame, 0 Make. There were Immo who said there was no difference between the two partim except in name— s remark which was anything but correct, and which they would find one bye Tittle further observation on their part. lie thought il they au ustituted falrplay for the won,' Libera m lis or a policy that wanted to give equal rights to all men no matter what position or nationality they belonged to. there WOuld be no difficulty in understanding what Liberal prin- nip'. were. The essayist then proceeded to review the actions of the two political parties commencing with 159 C, about the time when the Reform Bill or agitation was at its height. In contrasting the Liberal finance with that of the Torte, he said that during Mr tiladstowe's five wears of office the net reduction of the National Debt was £98,100,919, Lad the net remimion of taxes £12,451,41:08, nuking a total relief o! £38,648,217 or compared with the £17.1.425 of an increased taaation during Lord Beaconsfield's five years. After touching upon the fore* policy of the Government, which lie condemned, he concluded with a request that every one prermt wont! do his beet to remove one of the most un- scrupulous Premiers of England had during the present century, and to replace him by the man whose motto was wße just and fear not." A abort dixussion then took place In which Masers. Chas. dohnson,T. Chadwick, and Jae. Fogg took part.

M we were separating one goal friend volun- teered the statement that they were In for a dose of politic.. c 'The Lecturer did not like to olisappoint anybody. so if he happened to talk politics they must blame their friend for , it and not him. Another ventured to assert that the lecture . would be something very different from that, as political r Home Rule seas outside the lecturer's aympathies, and he r was a great drnl -nore likely to talk about husbands and , wives. It might, perhaps, interest them to know that the , . friernis who were with him in carrying on of those Sunday • afternoons at the Old 51111,• met him from time , to time in all sorts of places and under all sorts and circumstances with the question, "What are , your next three eubjects." And if, as was very frequently . the case, he had no subject at all in his mind ho had to in- , vent one on the spur of the moment or else submit to have , one invented for him, to that an announcement might be , made. This in a measure explained why such queer title. were announced from time to time. Nobody was to blame for the very nature of the 33,13 made it necessary. It, was : quite free to confess that if he knew what people expected , him to say he would de his very best to say eomething . different, because it was very unpleasant to talk to sleeping . people, especially when the speaker knew they were losing nothing. Ile went into 3 shop on Thurvity and a gentle- man said, " What is this Home Rule you are going to talk about; you will have that placefull of Irishmen." (Laugh- ter ) Well," he said, "why not, they once. good to talk to as any other inen,and if they come they shall hear a few words about that special form of Home Rule which is interesting to them," and so although he was not going to talk at any length about the demand which was made too a portion of the population of Ireland for a Government which should Is) independent of the British Par- liament, yet lie did desire to keep faith with any who might have come there under the imprernion that the Irish demand for Home Rule would be referred to. What the future of that country might be it was impossible to tell, and what arrangements might be made in the future for its good government it was perhaps useless to specnlate now: but for the tinle being Ireland woe an integral part of the British empire, and im inhabitants had unquestionably , just an strong a claim upon the synmatliy,go.al goyerimient, and beneficent legislation 01 (1,, British Parliament, as W 33 possessed by llor Majesty'a subjects in any and every other , part of the realm. It Wll3 nothing short of absolute folly to allow prejudice to interfere with the achninietration of handed justice and the sooner Englishmen and Irishmen , unitedly remlved to abolish the miserable jealousy which j sometiMes existed between them, the better it would be for r all concerned. Since oe were all citizens of one great j Uoited Kingdom we ought to rejoice in the j mutual interest and prosperity of the whole of , the inliabibants, and wherever inquiry into grievances , would promote a more complete understanding of Gat which would secure the greatest happiness of the , greatest number, such enquiry became at once a fluty and a privilege for all who were true lovers of their country and of , their kind. He then spoke of Home Rule iu its dom. , mune, referring to its exerci,e in the home of our child- , hood and passing on to consider it in our owo houses. , Perhaps enough had been said to indicate the sort of in- , duenee which was most likely to promote peace in the palace and contentment in the cot. It was the silken cord , of love which bound at closely tooter parents in our early , days; it was the sweet muaic of a voice which breathed a mother's love that woke our hearts to melody in the days of "Auld Lang 8y.."; it was the brightness of an eye that , beamed with love that melted us into tenderness when we breathed the story of a heart', devotion and sought to win a lady's band, and it was love that TM still powerful, the true , philosopher's shone turning all it touelivi into gold, and gilding with a radiance which seemed half dGine the com- moneat affairs of the daily IGes of men.

TEA PARTY AND MEETING. The annual m.ting in connection with the Soot of Temperance was held on Tuesday evening in the Old Mill, Liverpool-road, St. Helens A tea was orovided, after which a meeting wao held, presided over by Mr. J. S. Leach, who was supported on the platform by the Rev. H. J. Weather- bead, Mr. J. l'rescott, of F.arlestown, and Mr. Anderton (secretary). There was a fair attendance. The CHAIRMAN mid that he thonglot some individual more particularly connected with the Order should have had the honour of presiding and taking the mon prominent part at their annual meeting. But, if he were not a Son of Temperance as they underst.d it in connection with that Order, he won, anol he hoped he alwaye woould be, in a wider and broader .nse. There had been a vast amount of tem- perance work carried on mince the men t.k that building for promoting temperance. and it Ott. pleasure to remem- ber that teniperance meetings were still being carried on there ; and, although dotlicultim had to be contended with and struggles overcome, they wow still found there that I night. As true pone and (toughiere of temperance, he hoped I they would be faithful, and always he found with tlvoir colours unstained. The Sons of Temperance Order NM a movement which stood very prominently amongst friendly societies, and the Registrar-General admitted that the Sons of Temperance were pre-eminent and were growing more wealthy, which was a very good piece of testimony. The funds Store accomulating, and the institution was becoming comparatively the richest in the country. To be conn.ted with that temperance outer was to Ce connected with a thoroughly round institution. The bask of the Sons of Temperance Orkler he believell to be solhl and good, and woulot reflect credit on its founders in years to come. There were public-house clubs that could not bury their members when drool, and if an epidemic broke out among theon they would go out like the snuff of a candle. In tenqoerance friendly societies he believed he was right in saving float there seas no danger whatever of anything like that ever taking place. Teetotalers as a rule died in the ordinary way. Teetotalers were well known as being respectable. Outsiders thought they constituted the respectable portion of society, but they did not, and they said even if they were not teetotalers it did not matter ; they did not injure or meddle with the teetotalers. But he (the speaker) con. tended they did. It MIA only floe night previous that omen was taken in charge, toot lie inquired whether he was a teetotaler. He found that he was not. It was pre- posterous to think of a teetotaller being taken in charge.. The follow had been rushing to get in the train and lois life was in jeopardy, and if it haol not been for someone in the train 'Mooting for the train to stop, he might have been killed. He felt the effects of that unusual ehouting now— it was nonsense to say that teetomlere did not suffer by the foolishness of drinkers—and one woman pulled out a brandy bottle awl asid if it had not been for that she would have sunk. (Laughter.) Mr. Pitesower, of Earlestown, compared the early temperance reformers to such like noon as Howard and Wilberforce, who carried on their work with enerKv and epirit. In covef of time Banda 011101,0 seem formed, and ns time rolled on the Goal Teinplar and other institutions some into exietence. Being emboldened boy their succms, they began to proclaim their prioc'ples from the pulpit, and to-day those principles were advocated at the ballot box all through the country; and lie believed success would attend their efforts in thatdirection. As they passed on they feund that eomething else might be done, and though the battle had been longand tierce. yet they remembered that :-- Freedom's battle epee begun. Friends of tent/ser- ance began to see there was a great evil surrounding friendly societies in this country. They doubtless saw that when corns of their members came to pay their contributions at the public-house, where the meetings were very often held, thee were tempted to drink, and instead of @pending their eluls money only thee spent their entire earnings. But the Sons of Temperance -society was formed, by which each member got a legitimate share of benefits, instead, as in the old way,: the profita being eaten up by me section of the mciety, who brought disease upon themselves by their drinking habits. He had found that in the Bradford district the average sick- ness of the Rechabites per man for the last seven years was four days and two hours; whilst among the Oddfellows over the some period the average was 13 day. 10 hours per man. The death rate amongst the Oddfellows was one in 44, the Rechahites one in 141—three Oddicllows had died to one Rechabite. What was being done in friendly societies was also being done in omomme nacieties, and the statistics wrre in favourer the teetotallers.

EATEN BY SEUnC.9.—The Rangoon °crafts records a sad acurrekee at Port Blair :—On the evening of Christmas Day one of the 89th Regiment, named Kenney, went out to the ley to have a ewim—a daily recreation betemen dye and six p.m. When he was out a distance of about 130 yards from the Jetty he found himself attacked by a small ellsrk, which bit off one of the fingers of his left hand and lacerene4 anotbor and the thumb. The man being a good 51611111.1 bravely resisted the attadk and had nearly eucceeded in choking, it is said, his enemy, when he fonnd himself attacked by a larger monster, which seized him below the cap of the right knee, pouting an incision of about for, inches long by two deep. The wounded man atilt fought hie way bravely, swimmtng towards shore with his right hand, while with his other mutilated one he defended himself. While doing to the Recond and fiercer antagonist managed to seize his wounded leg Jun behind the knee-cap, rendering it per- fectly useless. lAte, howeveble tweet, and notwithstanding bit crippled condition, Kenney struggled on towards a boat be tow coming to his aid, when a third shark attacked him from behind, and tore of nearly the whole of the tech from his back. Even In this dreadful state he nunaged to swlm some 50 yards farther and to reach the boat before-mentioned,' when he was picked up. He was immediately conveyed to shore, laid in a doolie, and carried to the hoepitel, where ha received every care and attention but after lingering for 30 hours, and suffering the greeted t agony, he expired. When the corpse was examined the intestines were plainly visible through the exposed ribs, three or four of which were broken. The dimeneions of the lam bite were seen lob. 14 loci.. by It. The deceased was only 284 years of age.

There had been no competition in barrel piering; it was only by great exertion that one ROL of the men were got for one pier. The prizes were good, but the officers mid that the pier or,, so badly put together that it was really no pier at all. He was sorry for that, but he hoped they would do better. They used to have • mime for barrel piering, bet if the men would not torn up thee could not be expected to learn. A prier was, however, ar;arded to Colour-Sergeant Major Thompson.

Erecting a Tripod No. 3 Company won this prize, the detachment being Sergeant T. Ntylor, W. Naylor, Sapper Travis,and Sapper Pennington. The total amount gir en in prizes was £39 19s. Of. tacit. save of the prises given at Chtistanaa. Captain Ussly said it was his tdeasing duty to propose a vote of thanks to their worthy Anti esteemed Colonel. (Cheers.) He would not trespass unneceeearily upon their time, but it would be ungrateful on their part if tho rushed off to dancing without thanking hiln for providing there with that entertainment, which clearly demonstrated that he pleased and suisfieti with their conduct, week, and attendance during the past year. (Cheers.) At the same tone he must ask them to make manifest to him their high appreciation of the able, kind, efficient, energetic, and in- defatigable manner in which be had conducted the ntiaire of the corps since he had taken command. Many of them would remein'yer that at that thee that corps was an in- significant and despised little corps. But look at it now it had increased in number and in efficiency and, com- paring with what it was last year, they would err an almost incredible improvement in its financial state. Great credit was due to the colonel for the present success of the corps. What use was the crew of the vessel if its commander was not efficient and able to steer them front the rocks and difficulties which came in the way. Colonel Itothwell deserved all praise and all the assiebstace they could give him in the future.

div.p: ANNUAL SOIREE OF THE 2ND ST. HELENS.

The asnual pine of the 2nd L.E.V. was held on nom- day night, in the Engineer Hall, Croppers Hill. The hall was tastefully decorated with flags—the British, St. (Mores P Brazilian, Captain Marryat's Code, do—end they were ' arranged by Sergeant-11161or F. G. Bums Lieut. Brookes, and Sergeant-Instructer Goss. This was the first occasion the hall was decorated for the annual soiree, the flags having been lent by the kindness of several residents in the town. At half-past see an excellent tea was pro- vided by Mrs. Scrymgeour, to which about 250 rank and file eat down. Amongst those lament were—Col Bothwell, Capt. and Adjutant Curry, Captain Campbell, Captain Duffy, Captain Riga, Captain Craik, Lieutenant Moncrieff, Lieutenant Pendlebury, Lieutenant Crooks, Lieutenant Iddiechnie, Lieutenant Massey, sub-Lieutenant Brooker. There was also a lair sprinkling of ladies—Mrs. Campbell, Mrs. Crooke, Mrs. Brookes, Mrs. B. Itoughsedge, Mies Craik, bliss Irving, Miss McKechnie, nod Mizs McKenzie. Too having iltee dispennst with, the °dicers of the corps and a number of theladiesarranged themselves°ne platform which had been erected for the purpose and no Colonel Bothwell rising to speak he was Neely.] with vociferous cheers. lie said he had very great pleassve to meet them once more on that auspicious occasion. This was the occasion on which be felt the greatest pleasare in the year. This was tlie only occasion on which the hard workers of the carps came to receive their rewards. Irene not much that the volunteers did get generally. These rewards wore for the onerous work they did, and they tried all they could for them. He must ask them, before he commenced to distri- bute the pries, to give a vote of thanks to the prize donors. They hod been very liberal this vmr, and in consequence hail enabled Lim lobe very Illoeml also, toward the corps, Ile would ask the,,, to show it in the ueual way. by giooog "three tunes three." A hearty vote of thanks having been given, Colonel Bothwell went on to say that in intelelling there bad been 0 com- petition scarcely ; only two competed, and one of them was absent but he had no 'doubt he would tarn up when he would receive the prise. 7-he first prize (.23) was obtained be Company Sergeant-Major Present, and the second IT2I by Sergeant I'. The prisoner inn watchmaker, and was in the hahit of visit- ing Dempsey's house, anl prior to the 27th January he worked in company with Dempsey, afterwards going to lit. Helens to work for the father of Dempsey's master. Prisoner, about the 25th January. went to prosscutor's house, the latter letting him have his watch to ch.m. On the following day primner went again to the house,md said he had cleaned it, but also said he would bring it on the following day after he lied "thned" it. It. never turned up As proinised, and it •was afterwards found that he had pledged the watch at Mr. Edgar Valentine Morton's shop. —Prisoner pleaded guilty and was sent tor three months to prison with hard labour.—Williani Jones, Mr. Morton's , assistant, applied to the Bench to be refuncled for what he ' had lost by the transaction, hut he was informed that he did not exercise due precaution in receiving the watch, and that it was one of the risks of the trade, over which they had no control.

COMPLIMENTS TO INSPECtOR BUCKLEY. At the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, the Chairman (Mr. John litaadritt) 'aid that before the busine!Ja of the court was completed that day he should like to make • few remarks, which ho might cry were called forth he his seeing that Inspector Dutton, the sucuswar to Inspector Buckley, had cornmenc,d his duties The late Inspector hot been connected with the Runcorn force for 80 many years that his narne had become almost a household word amongst the people; and by his straightforward conduct, and the dili- gent Attention he had paid to his duties, he had gained the esteem not only of the magistrates on the bench,lent of the public at large. He might my that be had reason to know that the Chief Constable of the county had the highest opinion of Mr. Buckley'e abilities. Though the late Inspec- tor had alwaya lawn ready to punieh any wrong-doer,he had often shown much discretion by giving f 411114 and valuable advice to people in the town who might In eve been inclined to bring their petty aquabbles before the Bench, te try and arrange their diffejencee witlmut going to law. Inspector Buckley had teenier the poi.. force for the long period of 25 years, and had well earned the superannuation granted him. Ile was sure that the ,110,1 WWIon of all connected with the court would go with him in hie retirement, which they all hoped he might long live to enjoy. He had made those remarks, beuuse lie drought it Wail only right that eon. reference ahould be made to amok' and esteemed officer on his retiring from the force after so many years' service.— Mr. Garrett I can onlv my that during the short time I have occupied the office of Magistrates' Clerk, Inepector Buckley toe given me every :whitenrc in the discharge of my duties and I one him this acknowledgment, which I am very glvl to tender him. From my own experience, I am sure that I can support every word which Mr. Brundritt has uttered.--Superintendent Williamson • Mr. Brundrit, behalf of OW ',Slice, permit nie to say that I feel very grate- ful for the very kind remarks which you have made with respect to Inspector Buckley. I can endorse all the Awry, dons of your Worship, as fnspector Buckley has been acorn efficient officer, and it is wide regret Hat we lose hie services in the force.

Had the Committee ap- pointed a few months elm to deal with the complaints of Major Cartwright been invited be him to consider their I nature and origin they would have known, as other persons know, that much dissatisfaction prevailed nt the lloard by reason of the frequent journeys of the Master to Ireland. The alleged negligences count seven in number. They date back to the year 1875. The first Is the case of MeThye so repeatedly named to the Board. Since the notice of motion, I have traced the chargeability back to its origin and found the ease to have been first referred to by Major Cartwright in April, 1877. The pirticulars had left my mind, and I had no recollection as the man referred loin April, 1877 It is painful of MeThye to find, for the old man with reference to whose charge- ability the Board were so long without peace telt the removal from this country, in which he lived tor many years most acutely, batst gfave wrong her been done to him and to the famine stricken district in Galway to which heir removed. It is cleat that prior to his chargeability in 1875,1 he arquirol the status of irremovability, and the decision of the Board was to that effect on his admission and on the enquiry made in 1877, a decision with whinla Mojor Cart. weight concurred. The case calls for serious enqulry. The second negligence attributol is "Bridget Golden and child. admitted Ist December, 1876, and left when she was told she would be removed) 11th July, 1877, two of them over seven months in the Rouse." The particulars of this cane will be within the recollection of several Guanlians. The statement in the paper is grossly incorrect. The woman gave birth to her child in December, 1876, and had hey been removable it would have been an act of cruelty to hove removed thein before the spring. The mother appear.' several timee before the Board, who had no power to remove her, and who never pretended they had. They consented on e ich occasion to her staying a little time longer, and inally she was told the permisaion would not be repeated. The next Irish case in the list nada, "Winifred Moon end child, admitted 23n1 July, 1877, and tlischatzol Both September, 1879; two of them over two years in the house. This woman took her discharge when she found she was going to be removed." The record is wholly misleading, and hears internal evidence that ills no. Critil a few weeks back I had no knowledge of Winifred Moon, for whose re- moval no order had been made. On tracing the cane to the admission, I find the entry in the relief order book to be in the handwriting of Mr. Mackey. and no order for her removal was made. Her child was born subsequent to her admission, and how they came to be detained in the Work- house for over two years without the attention of the Gunflintns heing drawn to them it is not for the Clerk to explain. Why the case of Patrick Hating, aged 34, removed in August, 1878, to Ireland in included in the list is not clear The man Wes 90 troubled with hart legs and feet as to be scarcely able to walk.
