OLIVER CROMWELL'S FIGIIT AT WARRINGTON.

A correspondent of the Newastle Weekly leoxide in an acvannt of “Cromwell in Lancashire" mentions • few inter- esting incidents connected with the redoubtable Cromwell's I visit to Warrington. After describing the defeat at Preston by Cromwell and his Ironsides of the Royalist forces, who I were under the osinmand of the Duke of Hamilton and Sir Marmadtike Langdale, and the retreat of the Doke with his I army to Wigan and Warrington, hotly pursued by Cromwell, the writer save The Duke.of Hamilton, being hotly premed, made a final stand at the PAM of Winwiwk, near Warrington, where another dmperate and final conflict ensued. On the testi- mony of CrOmwell himself, the Royalists maintained the Pass with great rearilmion for many hours, hut they were ultimately defeated with great slaughter. At kast one I thousand Royalists were left dead on the field, and about two thounand were taken prisoners. The Duke, with the re- I mains of his cavalry, about three thoimand men, fied over ! the Mersey into Cbmhire, and left his infantry to the tender mercies of the victors. The reault was that Lieutenant- Ureneral Boiley, with the remains of the infantry, about four thousand men, surrendered at discretion in Warrington to the victorious Cromwell. Monroe and his Irishmen fl,d into Cumberland, as also did a tart of Sir Matineduke Langdale's forces, which afterwards capitulated at Appleby. The campaign one brief but decisive. In three days the Royalist army of 21.000 men was defeated and nearly destroyed hen force a little more than one-third of their number, and with a loss on the part of Cromwell of scarcely film men—a figure which seems almost incredible when the demean 1 protracted tights at Preston and Winwick are Laken into account. The Parliamentary lom must certainly be greatly onlereatimated. The only .01fieer of note slain under Cromwell was Colonel Thornhaugh. whose spirited horse carried him into the midst of the flying enemy, by whoin he was slain. Two years afterwards the Duke of Hamilton, with another large arniy, pass.l through Lanca- shire with Charles the Second, who had been proclaim.' King. Cromn-ell eras again soon on the track of the Royal army, which he nearly came up with in Lancashire. But his "crowning mercy,”/IS he himself termed it, WAS reserved for Worcester, where he finally overtook bin enemy, arid the hopes of Charles, for the time being. were shattered at a blow on the bloodstained field, and he himself narrowly es- coped capture by ceucesling himself at Buscobel, where he fled with a few devoted lel lowers alter the fight on Severn- side. The unfortunate Earl of Derby, after his defeat at Wigan Lane by Colonel Lilburne,only reached Worcester in time to participate in the defeat of hia royal master, and where he only escaped dmth to fall under the natal Bolton.

iiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii of Warrington, in • paper on the siege of that town during the Civil Warn, published in the Transac- tions of the Lancashire and Cheshire Historic Society, gives aome interesting details of the siege, and of Cromwell's brief stay in the town after the battles of Preston end Winwick, and the surrender of the relics of the Royal army under Bailey. In Wartington there are still some relics of the picturesque architecture of the Civil War period. A low thatched house on the south side of Church-street—and the tine old church adjoining was much damaged by the Par. liamentary artillery during the aiege—is by tradition said to have been occupied by Lord Derby while he reaided in the town during the stormy period and the tradition it borne Oaf he the fact that the quaint and lowly structure k efill known as the Earl's Lalgings. tin the opposite side of the street is another ancient building, now converted into • tavern, and known as the General Wolfe. prior to which, and doubtlem up to the perial of Wolfe's death on the Heiglita of Abraham, Quebec, it bore the sign of the Spotted Leopard. It still, however, retains the name of Cromwell'', lodgings; and here, according to seraph-tongued tradition, "Noll [Cromwell, who hae bean described as the" Noll- of the cavaliers] lalged for three days in August, 1848, after the defeat and surrender of the relics of the Duke of Hamilton's army, aud after the latter had Bed, 0 bloody from helm to spur," aouthward with the remains of his cavalry. Tradition further assorts—..d with much probability when the habit's of the great wither are comidered—that Cromwell (not then vet Lord Protector) during his brief stay in the town at- ientl,d worship in the ancient Baptist Chapel at Hill Cliff, a atul a half distant from Warriegton ; and it is further said that one of his soldiers—a COMMOU eccurrence during the civil wars—occopied the pulpit upon the occasion. No doubt the stern soldier.preacher would regale the general and his hearers with an address, tooter varioes bead?, in the orthodox smite them hip and thigh" etyle, and bristling With wrested tests 'supposed to he appropriate to the occa- den. Another tradition current atnongst the congregation who still worship at Hill Cliffe Chapel ie to the effect that during the civil war troubles, a man and his wife, members of the congregation, suffered martyrdom (presumably for their religious tenets) by ortler of 1"a person of high authority in Warrington." Lord Derby is evidently the" penson" indicated. Dr. Kendrick had not been successful in finding any written record of the occurrence when collecting nuteriale for the coinpilation of his paper above referred to ; yet the tradition, he observes, is eingularly in . cooed with 3 passage in " Lane...hire's Valley of Achor," printed in the same year (18431, in which it is stated that the Royalists at Warrington killed "a godly man and him wife in their own house." 1,0031 tradition fur- ther asserts that most of the Parliamentary soldiers who fell in the Kittle at Stockton Heath, near Warrington, in 1643, where the Royalists under Lord Derby were the victors, were iuterred in the burial-ground of Hill Cliff Chapel. Porn after the battle of Stockton Heath, however, Warring- ton wan again in postaemion of the popular party, after having been besieged and bombarded for a week. According to the temper of the titne, the surrender of the town waa " itn- proved " in " Lancashire'. Valley of Achor," and certain marvellous incidents connected therewith are reconl.l by the Puritanic writer. One item may be cited m a eample of the marvellous " manifestations." " A Providence," mys tbrqaainfand7thir ilanieoU47,ri,,teur; "mtn.nu,,che,t,ot to eo woolusier, „vie; liLn halt musket shot of the town. It woe no great a calm that they could not work but the enemy would hear when some went to work others went to prayers; and God raised a great wind that took away the noise ; a Providence not altogether an- like what I have heard in Boston. The Chancellor gave orders to Boston ; before they breathed in that new world, the wellmffecbsd pray; after their prayers, • mighty wind forces its passage into the church, blown down the organs, broke theta, and stopped their breath." From the above it would seem that the Lancashire Presbyterians, like the Scottish Covenanters, hada pious horror at the organ. Even at the present day the Scottish Preebyterians cannot " stomach "the organ in their places, of worship, which they consider would be desecrated by the presence of the " kiet fu' o' whietles," as they term the instrument. By order of the Parliament, Cromwell', moat decisive vic- tory over the Duke of Hamilton in Lancashire was coin. , heated throughout England and Walke by solemn thanks- . giving on Thursday. I the 7th September, of the some year. A collection was also ordered to be matte at ! the same time 'for M3lliled eobliers and poor wasted , people of Lancashire." The frightful condition of the county, which hi; suffered so much from hostile armies from the commencement of the war, is graphically set forth in "a true representation of the present low and lamentable condition of the county of Lancaster, and particularly the towns of Wigan, Ashton, And other parts adjacent," dated 24th May. 1649, signed by the Mayor and Bailiff of Wigan, I and lour other Lancashire ministera. The subscribe, in I soliciting contributions from the charitable, state that "the hand of God is evidently seen stretched out upon the county, chastening it with a three-corded scourge of sword, peetilenee, and famine, all at once afflicting it. They have borne the heat and burden of a first and second war in an especial tnanner above otherparts of the nation. Throug,h them the two great bodies of thO late SoWlish and English armies passed, and in their very bowel, was the great B,llt- ing, bloodshed. and breaking. In this county hath the plague and pestilence been raging there these three years anti upwards, occasioned chiefly by the wars. There in • very great ecarcity of provisions, especially of all eor's of grain, particularly that kind by which tile county is most sustained, which is full sixfold the price that of late it bath teen. All trade. by which they ha, e been teach eupported, is utterly decayed: it would melt any good heart loran the numerous warms of begging poor, and the many (amities that pine away at home. not haying face, to beg. Very many now craving alms at other men's doors who were used to give elms at their doors—to see paten., nay death, appear in the cheeks of the poor, and often to hear of Rome found dead in their houses, or highways, for want el bread." Ph,, painful but n• 'mum truthful picture shows ro what dire extremity bad the people of Lancashire, the pool,' well a. the formerly well-to-do, been brought by the diem- I trom Civil War, the handiwork of an arjitrary king.

But the beginning of the end wm drawing near, and lar, mshire, with the rest of the country, was soon to be released from the horrors of internicine war and its drmd concomi- I tants, famine and pestilence. In the year 1650 Charles the Second—son of "the man whose head had rolled in blood I on the scaffold—arrived in Scotland. Having conciliated I the adherents of the Covenant, who were now the hitter enemies of Cromwell, the King, who through his unworthy life was prodigal of promisee, was coon at the head of an army of 14,000 men. His intention, speedily carri,d cot,l woe to march into England, where he naturedy expected to be joined by the Cavaliers. Lan...hire was again in a state of ferment, m it was known that Lord Derby wee making preparations to join the new King in Lancashire, and would have done so but for his crushing defeat at Wigan lane by Lilburue before the Scottish army arrived in the country. The local excitement canned in Lancaahire by theme warlike preparations woe heightened by a remarkedge appearance of parbelia in the city, which are descanted upon iv, tract of the period entitled. The True Ftelation •of Strange Appari- tions men in the Air on Monday. 25th February, 1650, in and about the Town of Bolton in the Moores." The ap- pearance is described at length. le seen at mid-day, at the time of the weekly market : and it ionic noticed in Hol- lingworth's Chronicle," with reference to the appenrance in Manchester. Instances of similar dismay and excitement caused by another phenomenon—the aurora bormlis—before and after this period. are also referred to in Hunter's "Life of Heywood." While the 'skyey portents " were alarming the people of Lancaahire, and recalling to their memory the horrors of the preceding cam- paigns. the King with his arrry—uoder the command of the Duke of Hamilton and 4eneral Lesliw—arrived at Preston en the 16th August. Stout Cromwell was, however, advancing from Scotland, and approaching Lancashire with an army of 10,000 upon hearing of which the Royalist army marched rapidly south, and crossed into Chmhire by Warrington Bridge. General Lunbert had been directed to break down Warrington Bridge, eon, to delay the march of the King's ermy and allow time for Cromwell to come no with his pureeing hone. "Had the ordm been executed." says the county historian (11a1ttesl, "iii' highly probable that the fate of Charles the Second might have Seen deter- mined, as was that of hie royal father, in Lancashire." Cromwell, in hot permit, me. joined at Preston by Generals Lambert and Harris., at the head of 8.000 cavalry. A later from lambert gives an eccount of a skirmish with the Royalists at Warrington Bridge. which he failed to break down. ft seems that Charles, "great at the eetreatine trade," marched over the bridge in the van of his only, with hi, own Life Guards In the fight on the bridge, been Lam- bert was compelled to give we before overwhelming nem. here, the Royediete, as they fell on, cried,. Oh. you rogues, we will be with you before Cromwell comes." The know- ledge that invincible "Noll" was immediately in their rear was no doubt an incentive to their valour t ut "Noll,. as the adverse party loved to term him, was 005 to be denied;

like a sleuth-hound, he fought hisenetnies to hay on the3rd September ; and the crowning mercy" of Woscester etToc- tlally knocked kingly p.wer on the head. till brought back again on the reactionary waves of the R, cora:ion.
